amendments.rule: The **substantival article** — `הַ` on a participle or adjective used as a noun — takes the pronoun the ASV supplies to make it substantival, and heads on that pronoun rather than on the relative that follows it. `הָרַע` → *that which was evil* is the article with *that which*, headed on *that*; `הָעֹשֶׂה` → *him that doeth* is the article with *him that*, headed on *him*. The supplied pronoun is the article's own rendering and is never `added`. The predicate word keeps its own English, including any copula the ASV supplies, which stays with it under rule 20: in *that which is right*, *is* and *right* belong to the adjective and only *that which* belongs to the article. **An attributive article the ASV renders by a relative goes the same way.** Where `הַ` stands on a participle or adjective modifying an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative instead of a *the* — `אֹיְבֶיךָ הַקָּמִים עָלֶיךָ` → *thine enemies that rise up against thee*, `הָאִישׁ הָרַךְ` → *The man that is tender*, `הַכְּתוּבִים` → *that are written*, `הַכֹּהֵן הַמְחַטֵּא` → *The priest that offereth* — the article takes that relative and heads on it, while the participle or adjective keeps its own English together with any supplied copula, exactly as above. **But read where the ASV has put the attributive before reaching for that sentence.** Where it renders the attributive prenominally instead, no relative stands before the attributive's own word and rule 47 governs the count: the phrase's single *the* is the first article's and the agreement article is `unrepresented`, as `הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ` → *the anointed priest* is. **A demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner the ASV writes in the article's place goes the same way, whatever the article stands on.** Where the ASV writes no *the* for the phrase but a *this*, *that*, *these*, *those*, a possessive *his*, *her*, *thy*, *thine*, or a quantifier such as *any* or *every*, standing where the phrase's *the* would stand — `הַזִּמָּה` → *this lewdness*, `הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thine elder*, `הַבֶּגֶד` → *any garment* — that word is what the ASV has written for the article: the article takes it and heads on it, and it is neither `added` nor a reason to mark the article `unrepresented`. A quantifying determiner is read on exactly the terms of the others and is not left to the noun under rule 15: that rule gives a supplied *any* to the nominal expression only where no determiner morpheme stands before the word it determines, and an article standing on that word is such a morpheme. **Read that as no *the* standing before the article's own word, not as no *the* anywhere in the phrase.** Where the article sits on the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain and the ASV writes a *the* before the construct and a demonstrative or possessive before the rectum's own word, rule 29's arthrous case governs the count: nothing is fronted, the article takes the determiner standing before its own word, and the construct takes the supplied *the*. `יְמֵי הַמִּשְׁתֶּה` → *the days of* ***their*** *feasting* gives *their* to the article and *the days* to the construct, exactly as `שְׂדֵה הָעִיר` → *the fields of the city* gives the second *the* to the article there. Do not mark such an article `unrepresented` and the determiner `added` under rule 18's closing sentence: that sentence governs a supplied possessive with no determiner morpheme standing before the word it determines, and here one does. **But only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner.** A pronominal suffix standing in the same phrase is rendered by a possessive of its own under rule 18, a `כֹּל` standing on the noun is itself what an *any* or an *every* renders under rule 15, an `אֶחָד` standing in the phrase is itself what a distributive *each* or *every* renders, and a demonstrative pronoun standing in the phrase is itself what a written *this*, *that*, *these* or *those* renders; where the ASV writes one determiner for the whole phrase that morpheme takes it and the article is `unrepresented`: `אֲחוֹתֵךְ הַגְּדוֹלָה` → *thine elder sister* gives *thine* to the suffix on `אָחוֹת` and leaves the article nothing, while `אֲחוֹתַיִךְ הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thy sisters, thine elder sisters* writes a determiner for each and the article takes the second; so too `אֲחִיהֶם הַבְּכוֹר` → *their eldest brother's*, where the suffix takes *their* and the article has nothing, and `הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *that place*, where `הוּא` takes the written *that* while the noun's article and the agreement article beside it are both `unrepresented` under rule 47. **And the morpheme that licenses the determiner need not stand inside the noun phrase.** What the preceding sentences ask is which morpheme the written determiner answers to, so read the clause rather than the phrase's edges: where a dative or possessive `לְ` with a pronominal suffix stands beside the noun and the ASV recasts it as a possessive determiner on that noun, the suffix is what the determiner realizes under rules 18 and 40, the `לְ` is `unrepresented` under rule 40, and the article is `unrepresented` exactly as it is beside a suffix written on the noun itself. `וַיְהִי לָהֶם הַגְּבוּל` → *And* ***their*** *border was* gives *their* to the suffix, *was* to `הָיָה` under rule 43, and nothing to either the preposition or the article. Do not hand such a determiner to the article on the ground that the suffix stands outside the phrase: that would leave the morpheme the ASV wrote the word for holding nothing, against rules 2 and 18. Count the determiners and read which word each stands before, as rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s. **The `אֶחָד` case is counted on exactly those terms, and it turns on the one word the ASV wrote rather than on where that word stands.** A distributive determiner stands precisely where the phrase's *the* would stand, so the preceding sentences alone would hand it to the article; the numeral takes it because the numeral is itself what the word says. Where the ASV writes one such determiner, it is the numeral's and every article in the phrase — the noun's own and the agreement article on the numeral alike — is `unrepresented`: `לַפָּר הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***each*** *bullock* and `לַכֶּבֶשׂ הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***every*** *lamb*. Where it instead writes a *the* before the noun and an *one* for the numeral, two determiners are written and each morpheme takes the one standing before its own word: `לָאַיִל הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***the one*** *ram* gives *the* to the noun's article and *one* to the numeral, the agreement article still `unrepresented` under rule 47. One verse may write both shapes, and NUM.28.12 and NUM.28.28 do. The corpus aligns `אֶחָד` to *each* in 18 units, to *every* in four and to *every one* in five, so a numeral standing in the phrase is a morpheme that licenses such a determiner; the article's own units of *every* are the case this sentence excludes, where no such numeral stands. **And a determiner another morpheme licenses is still a determiner standing before the article's own word.** The count above is unchanged where the preceding sentences have left the article with nothing: still nothing is fronted, and where such a phrase is the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain the construct takes a supplied *the* of its own. `שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *the name of that place* gives *the name* to the construct, *that* to the demonstrative pronoun, and nothing to either article. Do not read the article's silence as an anarthrous rendering and hand the construct's *the* back to it as a fronted determiner: what forces fronting under rule 29 is a rectum the ASV renders with no determiner at all — `לֻחֹת הָאֲבָנִים` → *the two tables of stone* — and a rectum whose own word carries a *this*, a *that* or a possessive is not that, whichever morpheme in the phrase the word answers to. Read what stands before the rectum's word, not which morpheme was left with nothing. Read what the ASV writes for the article and let that decide which rule governs: a bare *the* is rule 15's ordinary attributive article, a relative or a supplied pronoun is this rule's, a demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner is this rule's too, and where the ASV writes none of them the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29. Where coordinated attributives share a single written relative, the first article takes it and the rest are `unrepresented` under rules 22 and 47. **An articleless attributive that the ASV recasts as a relative clause keeps the supplied relative with the attributive itself.** Where an adjective or participle without an article modifies an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative frame — `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` → *a land that is unclean* — the attributive takes the relative together with its own English and any copula rule 20 supplies, headed on the word carrying its lexeme. The relative realizes the Hebrew attributive relation and is not `added`; rule 55's supplied clause subordinator is a different construction. **But read whether the Hebrew writes an attributive or a predication before reaching for that sentence.** What it governs is an adjective or participle standing with the noun it modifies inside one nominal expression, as `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` is. Where the adjective or participle is instead the predicate of a verbless clause and the ASV subordinates that clause to the noun standing as its subject, the English relative subordinates a clause rather than realizing an attributive relation, so rules 46 and 55 govern it: the relative answers to no morpheme and is its own `added` unit, while the copula and the predicate's own English stay with the adjective or participle under rule 20. `דּוֹר טָהוֹר בְּעֵינָיו` → *a generation* ***that*** *are pure in their own eyes* and `לַיִשׁ גִּבּוֹר בַּבְּהֵמָה` → *The lion,* ***which*** *is mightiest among beasts* both leave the relative `added` and give *are pure* and *is mightiest* to the adjective. Read the Hebrew clause rather than the English noun phrase the ASV has built around it, since a translation that subordinates a predication writes exactly what an attributive relation writes. Three things mark a predication. A subject or resumptive pronoun standing in the clause is one, as the `הֵם` of `אַרְבָּעָה הֵם קְטַנֵּי־אָרֶץ` → *four things* ***which*** *are little upon the earth* is. A further finite clause coordinated under the same English relative is another, since no attributive frame carries one. And a clause of the same shape elsewhere in the passage that the ASV renders as a main clause with a copula is the third, as `הַנְּמָלִים עַם לֹא־עָז` → *The ants are a people not strong* stands beside the `לַיִשׁ גִּבּוֹר` above. Where none of these is present and the Hebrew writes an attributive inside a nominal expression, the preceding sentence governs as before.
amendments.why: PRO.30 met the case rule 41's articleless-attributive sentence had not considered: an articleless adjective that is the predicate of a verbless clause, which the ASV subordinates to its subject with a relative. On the surface that is indistinguishable from `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` → *a land that is unclean*, so the sentence as written would hand the relative to the adjective, which conflicts with rule 46's ruling that a relative supplied for a clause juxtaposed to a written antecedent is not licensed by that rule, and with rule 55's count. The chapter analysed the same construction both ways — added at 30.12 and 30.24, folded into the adjective at 30.30 — which is the split this pass patched, so the qualification is what keeps a later pass from reproducing it. The amendment narrows the existing sentence where it stands rather than adding a cross-reference, and states the three tells the chapter actually used: the resumptive `הֵם` of 30.24, the coordinated finite clause of 30.12 and 30.30, and the parallel main-clause renderings of 30.25 and 30.26. It claims no corpus counts, because the packet carried none for this construction; the rule-41 units the corpus does hold are attributive ones, which the amended sentence still governs unchanged.

conventions: A relative the ASV supplies over a clause with a written antecedent and no relative morpheme is `added` throughout this chapter, including where the clause is verbless and its predicate an articleless adjective: 30.12, 30.24 and 30.30 all leave the relative added and give the copula and the adjective's own English to the predicate under rule 20. Rule 41's articleless attributive was deliberately not applied to such a predication, because the same Hebrew shape is rendered as a main clause at 30.25 and 30.26 and because the English relative's scope runs on over a coordinated finite clause at 30.12 and 30.30. Where a morpheme stands for the word it takes it instead: the resumptive suffixes of 30.14 and 30.18 under rule 18, and the written כִּי of 30.23 under rule 55.

The presentative *There is* / *There are* joins the anchor the ASV actually writes — דּוֹר at 30.11–30.14, or the substantival numeral with the supplied generic *things* at 30.15, 30.18, 30.24 and 30.29 — under rules 20 and 31, with the head staying on the numeral. The resuming הֵנָּה, הֵמָּה or הֵם is the unrendered occurrence and is `unrepresented` under rule 22; only where a line writes no other subject does the pronoun take its own word, as the second הֵמָּה of 30.24 takes *they*. BSB attaches those pronouns, which accounts for four of the eight BSB disagreements and is a convention difference rather than an error.

A possessive determiner the ASV supplies where no morpheme licenses it is `added` under rule 18's closing sentence: *his father* and *his mother* at 30.17, *her hands* at 30.28, *their march* at 30.29, *thy hand* and *thy mouth* at 30.32. Where a determiner morpheme does stand in the phrase it takes the word instead, so the assimilated article of בַּשִּׂמְלָה at 30.4 takes the *his* of *in his garment* under rule 41. Read whether an article or suffix is present before marking such a word added.

In 30.27 `מֶלֶךְ אֵין לָאַרְבֶּה` → *The locusts have no king*, the possessive לְ takes the *have* under rule 43 and the existential אַיִן takes only the *no* under rule 50. The אַיִן is holding the word written for it and is not a home for a second one, and the same possessive לְ carries the *have* at 30.2 and the *hath* at 30.15, so the chapter reads all three the same way.

where the ASV writes one determiner for the whole phrase that morpheme takes it and the article is `unrepresented`: `אֲחוֹתֵךְ הַגְּדוֹלָה` → *thine elder sister* gives *thine* to the suffix on `אָחוֹת` and leaves the article nothing, while `אֲחוֹתַיִךְ הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thy sisters, thine elder sisters* writes a determiner for each and the article takes the second; so too `אֲחִיהֶם הַבְּכוֹר` → *their eldest brother's*, where the suffix takes *their* and the article has nothing, and `הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *that place*, where `הוּא` takes the written *that* while the noun's article and the agreement article beside it are both `unrepresented` under rule 47. **And the morpheme that licenses the determiner need not stand inside the noun phrase.** What the preceding sentences ask is which morpheme the written determiner answers to, so read the clause rather than the phrase's edges: where a dative or possessive `לְ` with a pronominal suffix stands beside the noun and the ASV recasts it as a possessive determiner on that noun, the suffix is what the determiner realizes under rules 18 and 40, the `לְ` is `unrepresented` under rule 40, and the article is `unrepresented` exactly as it is beside a suffix written on the noun itself. `וַיְהִי לָהֶם הַגְּבוּל` → *And* ***their*** *border was* gives *their* to the suffix, *was* to `הָיָה` under rule 43, and nothing to either the preposition or the article. Do not hand such a determiner to the article on the ground that the suffix stands outside the phrase: that would leave the morpheme the ASV wrote the word for holding nothing, against rules 2 and 18. Count the determiners and read which word each stands before, as rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s. **The `אֶחָד` case is counted on exactly those terms, and it turns on the one word the ASV wrote rather than on where that word stands.** A distributive determiner stands precisely where the phrase's *the* would stand, so the preceding sentences alone would hand it to the article; the numeral takes it because the numeral is itself what the word says. Where the ASV writes one such determiner, it is the numeral's and every article in the phrase — the noun's own and the agreement article on the numeral alike — is `unrepresented`: `לַפָּר הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***each*** *bullock* and `לַכֶּבֶשׂ הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***every*** *lamb*. Where it instead writes a *the* before the noun and an *one* for the numeral, two determiners are written and each morpheme takes the one standing before its own word: `לָאַיִל הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***the one*** *ram* gives *the* to the noun's article and *one* to the numeral, the agreement article still `unrepresented` under rule 47. One verse may write both shapes, and NUM.28.12 and NUM.28.28 do. The corpus aligns `אֶחָד` to *each* in 18 units, to *every* in four and to *every one* in five, so a numeral standing in the phrase is a morpheme that licenses such a determiner; the article's own units of *every* are the case this sentence excludes, where no such numeral stands. **And a determiner another morpheme licenses is still a determiner standing before the article's own word.** The count above is unchanged where the preceding sentences have left the article with nothing: still nothing is fronted, and where such a phrase is the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain the construct takes a supplied *the* of its own. `שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *the name of that place* gives *the name* to the construct, *that* to the demonstrative pronoun, and nothing to either article. Do not read the article's silence as an anarthrous rendering and hand the construct's *the* back to it as a fronted determiner: what forces fronting under rule 29 is a rectum the ASV renders with no determiner at all — `לֻחֹת הָאֲבָנִים` → *the two tables of stone* — and a rectum whose own word carries a *this*, a *that* or a possessive is not that, whichever morpheme in the phrase the word answers to. Read what stands before the rectum's word, not which morpheme was left with nothing. Read what the ASV writes for the article and let that decide which rule governs: a bare *the* is rule 15's ordinary attributive article, a relative or a supplied pronoun is this rule's, a demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner is this rule's too, and where the ASV writes none of them the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29. Where coordinated attributives share a single written relative, the first article takes it and the rest are `unrepresented` under rules 22 and 47. **An articleless attributive that the ASV recasts as a relative clause keeps the supplied relative with the attributive itself.** Where an adjective or participle without an article modifies an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative frame — `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` → *a land that is unclean* — the attributive takes the relative together with its own English and any copula rule 20 supplies, headed on the word carrying its lexeme. The relative realizes the Hebrew attributive relation and is not `added`; rule 55's supplied clause subordinator is a different construction. **But read whether the Hebrew writes an attributive or a predication before reaching for that sentence.** What it governs is an adjective or participle standing with the noun it modifies inside one nominal expression, as `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` is. Where the adjective or participle is instead the predicate of a verbless clause and the ASV subordinates that clause to the noun standing as its subject, the English relative subordinates a clause rather than realizing an attributive relation, so rules 46 and 55 govern it: the relative answers to no morpheme and is its own `added` unit, while the copula and the predicate's own English stay with the adjective or participle under rule 20. `דּוֹר טָהוֹר בְּעֵינָיו` → *a generation* ***that*** *are pure in their own eyes* and `לַיִשׁ גִּבּוֹר בַּבְּהֵמָה` → *The lion,* ***which*** *is mightiest among beasts* both leave the relative `added` and give *are pure* and *is mightiest* to the adjective. Read the Hebrew clause rather than the English noun phrase the ASV has built around it, since a translation that subordinates a predication writes exactly what an attributive relation writes. Three things mark a predication. A subject or resumptive pronoun standing in the clause is one, as the `הֵם` of `אַרְבָּעָה הֵם קְטַנֵּי־אָרֶץ` → *four things* ***which*** *are little upon the earth* is. A further finite clause coordinated under the same English relative is another, since no attributive frame carries one. And a clause of the same shape elsewhere in the passage that the ASV renders as a main clause with a copula is the third, as `הַנְּמָלִים עַם לֹא־עָז` → *The ants are a people not strong* stands beside the `לַיִשׁ גִּבּוֹר` above. Where none of these is present and the Hebrew writes an attributive inside a nominal expression, the preceding sentence governs as before.
amended.why: PRO.30 met the case rule 41's articleless-attributive sentence had not considered: an articleless adjective that is the predicate of a verbless clause, which the ASV subordinates to its subject with a relative. On the surface that is indistinguishable from `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` → *a land that is unclean*, so the sentence as written would hand the relative to the adjective, which conflicts with rule 46's ruling that a relative supplied for a clause juxtaposed to a written antecedent is not licensed by that rule, and with rule 55's count. The chapter analysed the same construction both ways — added at 30.12 and 30.24, folded into the adjective at 30.30 — which is the split this pass patched, so the qualification is what keeps a later pass from reproducing it. The amendment narrows the existing sentence where it stands rather than adding a cross-reference, and states the three tells the chapter actually used: the resumptive `הֵם` of 30.24, the coordinated finite clause of 30.12 and 30.30, and the parallel main-clause renderings of 30.25 and 30.26. It claims no corpus counts, because the packet carried none for this construction; the rule-41 units the corpus does hold are attributive ones, which the amended sentence still governs unchanged.

report: Checked all 42 candidate lemma groups. Every multi-treatment bucket but one is the ASV rendering one morpheme differently in different contexts, which the source licenses: the waw's connectives (and, but, Yet, So, nor, Yea, Or) are read off the ASV under rule 14's open list; מִן is unrepresented at 30.7 (bare indirect object, rule 40), *from* at 30.8, and *too … for* at 30.18 (comparative, rule 24's degree-word sentence, headed on the relational word exactly as *more … than* is at 30.2); לְ is *have/hath* at 30.2, 30.15 and 30.27 (possessive, rule 43) and unrepresented at 30.8 (dative recast, rule 40); the article takes the written *the* where one stands, *his* at 30.4 where a possessive fills its slot (rule 41), *them that* at 30.5 (substantival, rule 41), and is unrepresented at 30.19 (indefinitely rendered rectum, rule 29) and 30.30 (no *the* written).

One real split, invisible to the lemma table because one side of it is an `added` unit. A relative the ASV supplies over a verbless clause whose predicate is an articleless adjective is `added` under rule 55 at PRO.30.12 (*a generation that are pure*) and PRO.30.24 (*four things which are little*), but at PRO.30.30 (*The lion which is mightiest*) it was folded into the adjective under rule 41's articleless-attributive clause. I patched 30.30 to match the other two: the Hebrew writes a predication rather than an attributive — the parallel clauses at 30.25–26 are rendered as main clauses with the copula on the predicate (`הַנְּמָלִים עַם לֹא־עָז` → *The ants are a people not strong*), and the English relative's scope runs on over the coordinated finite clause *And turneth not away*, which no attributive frame carries. Statuses after the patch: 26 added, 398 aligned, 11 unrepresented, 435 units.

The chapter's other twelve supplied relatives (30.11, 30.15 twice, 30.16 twice, 30.17, 30.18, 30.21, 30.24, 30.29 twice, and now 30.30) all stand over clauses with written antecedents and no relative morpheme, and are `added`. The three that are not added rest on morphemes that are there: the *whose* of 30.14 and the second *which* of 30.18 on resumptive suffixes under rule 18, and the *that* of 30.23 on a written כִּי under rule 55. That division holds and needed no change.

BSB: none of the eight disagreements is an error. Four (הֵנָּה, הֵמָּה, הֵם at 30.15, 30.18, 30.24, 30.29) are the tripartite resuming pronoun the ASV leaves unrendered, `unrepresented` under rules 20 and 22; BSB attaches it. Three (בְּ 30.6 *reprove thee*, מִן 30.7 *Deny me them*, לְ 30.8 *Give me*) are rule 40 recastings, each a named case in that rule. One (הַ 30.19) is rule 29's indefinitely rendered rectum: the ASV writes *of an eagle*, so nothing is fronted and the construct takes a supplied *the*. No accepted edge was changed to move the rate.

Also checked and left alone: the italic comparative *as* of 30.14, given to both predicate nouns under rule 33 and treated the same way twice; the *up*, *forth*, *out* and *away* particles of 30.4, 30.13, 30.17, 30.27, 30.30 and 30.33, each completing a lexeme the bare English verb does not write under rule 44; and the light-verb heads of 30.5, 30.8, 30.9, 30.22, 30.23, 30.28 and 30.32, which land on the verb or the complement according to rule 44's subtraction test rather than by position (so *use profanely* heads on *use* while *taketh hold* heads on *hold*, both from the same lemma תָּפַשׂ).

I considered promoting the אֵין לְ division of 30.27 — *have* to the possessive לְ under rule 43, *no* to the existential אַיִן under rule 50 — and did not. Rules 43, 50 and 51 already decide it by counting the ASV's words against the morphemes that could carry them, and the packet carries no corpus evidence for that pairing; it is recorded as a chapter convention instead.
